entries.narration: This is where the course ends: book shop, an online shop for books, running on A W S, and taking an order. The map on the left is the whole thing, drawn the way A W S draws its own diagrams: a Region in London, a network spread across three availability zones, the app running in containers, a database, queues, a lake for reports, and the controls an account needs. Every part of it is declared in code, and every part is built, one section at a time, in the courses that follow. The terminal on the right is the finished shop at work. The app answers a request for a book's page: Night Trains of Europe, by Ana Lima, ten ninety nine, forty in stock. Then a shopper checks out. The order is recorded in the database, in one transaction, and a single event is published: order placed. The last command asks who heard it. The fulfilment queue did, so the book will be packed. The points queue did, so the shopper earns loyalty points. The fraud check did not: it only listens for orders of five hundred pounds or more, and this one was ten ninety nine. The side pane draws that path. One honest note, which applies to the whole course: A W S here is an emulator running on this machine, while the app and the database are real. Every frame that shows emulated output says so. The commands, the code and the Terraform are exactly what you would run against a real account. Next, why anyone would rent all of this instead of owning it.

Before A W S, a shop like this bought its servers. The question was always how many, and the answer was always: enough for the busiest hour. The plot is a model of one day of the shop's traffic, labelled as one. Sixty requests a second overnight, two hundred and forty through the day, and a peak of five hundred and sixty at six in the evening. Bought for that peak, the shop owns six servers, each handling a hundred requests a second, and all six run all day, busy or not. That is the flat line. Renting, the other line follows the day: one server overnight, more through the day, ten at the peak, because rented servers are kept about sixty percent busy, the rule Course 6 will explain. The terminal is the model's own output, hour by hour. The table sums it up. Owned: a hundred and forty four server hours a day, paid for whether used or not, for years. Rented: eighty four, paid for by the hour. And when a day is busier than planned, owned capacity turns shoppers away, while rented capacity adds servers in minutes. The trade is real, and the last row says it: renting gives up control of the hardware itself. You choose the size and the place, never the machine. For a shop whose busiest hour is ten times its quietest, renting wins by a long way. Next, what we will build, course by course.

Here is the map again, and beside it the plan. Twelve courses, and after each one the shop can do something it could not do before. The next course stays with A W S itself: what a Region is, what happens when you make a request, what an A R N names, who is responsible for what, and what costs money. Course 3 starts the project: an account, a profile, and Terraform, with its state kept safely in a bucket. Course 4 secures it: a role for the app, and policies proven to deny what they should. Course 5 builds the network: a V P C across three zones, a load balancer, a name and a certificate. Course 6 runs the app in containers on Fargate, tested and scaled. Course 7 gives it data: carts, orders and photos, and the last book in stock sold only once. Course 8 decouples the checkout with queues, events and a payment workflow. Course 9 ships every change through a pipeline, to development and then to production. Course 10 answers what the shop sold yesterday, from a lake. Course 11 operates it: metrics, alarms, an audit trail, keys, a firewall, backups and an incident. And Course 12 measures it, prices it, and reviews it. The note is the rule that holds all of it together: from Course 3 on, every part is declared in Terraform, and every section builds on the one before. One shop, from an empty account to this map. Next course: how A W S runs a request.

A W S is not one place. It is Regions, and the shop will live in one of them: E U West 2, London. The frame draws it as A W S draws a Region, with a dashed border, because a Region is a place, not a thing you create. Inside it are three availability zones, A, B and C. Each zone is one or more data centres, with its own power, cooling and network, far enough from the others that a flood or a fire in one does not reach the next, and close enough for fast links between them. The terminal asks the Region for its zones, and gets the three names, each with a zone I D. The names are per account; the I D names the same physical zone for everyone. This answer comes from the emulator, which answers the way the A P I does. To the right, outside any Region, are edge locations: hundreds of smaller sites around the world, close to shoppers, which serve cached content and answer name lookups. The table is the reason for all of this: what fails together, and what survives it. A server fails, and anything keeping two copies carries on. A data centre fails, and its zone's other buildings carry on. A whole zone fails, and only a system running in two or three zones carries on, which is why the shop will run in all three. A whole Region is the largest failure, and Course 11 comes back to it. Next, which services live where.

Every A W S service has a scope, and the scope decides what it fails with. The frame places the services the shop will use on the same Region picture. At the top, global: I A M, which holds users, roles and policies; Route fifty three, for names; and CloudFront, the edge. There is one of each for the whole account, everywhere. Inside the Region, Regional services: an S three bucket, an S Q S queue, a Lambda function, a DynamoDB table. Each lives in E U West 2, and A W S spreads it across the Region's zones for you, so losing one zone does not lose your bucket. At the bottom, zonal: an E C two instance and a subnet each live in exactly one zone, and so do a disk and a database instance. If that zone fails, they fail with it. The table draws the consequence. Global services almost never fail, but a change to them can take a while to spread, so the shop creates its roles once and leaves them. Regional services need nothing more from the shop inside the Region. Zonal things are the shop's job: if it wants to survive a zone, it must run one in each zone, which is why it will have a subnet, a task and a N A T gateway in each of three zones. Next, how every one of these services is actually asked to do anything.

Whatever you do in A W S, you do by calling an A P I. The console in a browser is a web page that calls it. The command line is a program that calls it. An S D K, such as boto three for Python, is a library that calls it. And Terraform, which builds the shop from Course 3 on, calls it through the S D K for Go. The frame draws four ways to ask, and one place they all go: a single H T T P S endpoint for the service in the Region, here S three in E U West 2, which then does the work. The terminal asks the same question two ways. First, the A W S C L I lists the account's buckets. Then three lines of Python ask exactly the same thing, through boto three. Both get the same answer: an empty list. This is a fresh account, in the emulator, and nothing has been made yet. The table says why this matters for everything that follows. Anything the console can do, code can do, because the console is code. And code can be read, reviewed, repeated and put in version control, which is how this course will build the shop: never by clicking. Next, what one of those requests actually looks like on the wire.

Here is the list buckets request from the last section, taken apart. A small script asks boto three to show the request just before it is sent, exactly as signed. It is an H T T P S get, to the S three endpoint in London. Then come the headers that matter. The date and time, because a signed request is only valid for fifteen minutes, so a captured one cannot be replayed tomorrow. A hash of the body, which is empty here, so the body cannot be swapped on the way. And the authorisation header, signature version four, in three parts. The credential names whose key signed it, and for which day, Region and service. Signed headers lists what the signature covers. And the signature itself: a value computed from all of that and the secret key. The secret key is never sent. The answer comes back: two hundred, and no buckets. The table goes part by part, and the row of steps below says what A W S does on arrival. T L S first, so you know you are talking to A W S. Then the signature is recomputed from the same parts with the same secret: if it matches, the request really came from the key's owner, unchanged. Then I A M decides whether that principal may list buckets. Only then does S three answer. The clock in this course is fixed, so the signature is the same on every run. Next, the names every one of these requests uses.

Every resource in A W S has a name that is unique across all of A W S: an Amazon Resource Name, or A R N. The top of the frame is its shape, using the queue the shop will make in Course 8: six fields, separated by colons. The word A R N. The partition, which is A W S almost everywhere. The service that owns the name. The Region. The account. And the resource itself, often a type and a name. A small script splits three real ones. The first is the caller, as the emulator names it: a user called moto, in the development account. No Region, because I A M and S T S identities are global. On A W S, alex's session would read assumed role, book shop developer, alex, and the note says so. The second is a policy that A W S itself maintains, read only access. Its account field says A W S, because it belongs to no customer. The third is the bucket Course 3 will make, book shop catalog. Its Region and account are both empty: a bucket's name is already unique across every account in the world, so it needs neither. Those empty fields are worth reading, because they tell you the scope of the thing, the same scopes as two sections ago. A R Ns are what policies are written in: allow this principal, this action, on this A R N. Course 4 writes them. Next, who is responsible for which part of all this.

When the shop runs on A W S, who is responsible for what? The answer is shared, and where the line falls depends on the service. The table is the stack, from the bottom up, for the four kinds of service the shop uses. The bottom row is always A W S: the buildings, the hardware and the network. The top row is always yours: the data, and who may read it. A W S will never decide who may read your bucket; that is your policy. In between, the line moves. With an E C two instance, a server you rent, almost everything is yours: the operating system and its patches, the runtime, your code, and how many servers to run. With containers on Fargate, A W S runs the operating system and places the containers; you bring the container, and choose how many. With Lambda, A W S runs nearly everything, including the runtime you pick; you bring a function. And with S three, you bring only data and its policy. The row of services below draws the same line moving: from E C two to S three, there is less to run. Less to run is less to patch at three in the morning. It is also less control, which is the same trade as owning against renting, one level up. The shop uses all four, each where it fits. Next, the last thing to understand before building: what costs money.

A W S charges by meters, and the surprise is usually which ones keep running. The lab takes one small server through a month, in three states, at hypothetical rates: round numbers chosen for the course, not A W S's prices, which you should always check. Running all month, it costs about twenty five dollars: the instance's time, its disk, its public address, and the data it sends out to the internet. Now stop it. Most people expect zero. It is about five dollars and sixty five cents, because two meters are still running: the disk still exists, and the public address is still held. Only terminating it, and letting the disk and the address go, brings it to zero. The bar chart shows the three months, and the table lists the meters and when each one runs. Instance time, only while it runs. Disk, while the volume exists, stopped or not. A public I P address, while you hold it. Data out to the internet, by the gigabyte. And requests, for services such as S three, each one counted. Two habits follow from this, and the course keeps both. Every resource carries tags saying what it belongs to, so the bill can be split. And a budget sends an alarm before the month surprises anyone. Course 3 sets both up on the very first day. That completes Course 2. Next course: starting the project.

Everything the book shop will ever run lives inside an A W S account, so before we build anything we need to know who can get into one, and how. On the left are the two kinds of people who sign in. Alex is the developer and signs in every day. The owner opened the account, once, with an email address and a password. That email and password are the root user, in red in the middle: the one identity that can do anything at all in the account, and that nothing inside the account can restrict. So the root user is locked away. It gets a strong password and multi factor authentication, it gets no access keys, and it is used only for the handful of jobs in the table on the right that nothing else is allowed to do: closing the account, changing its email or name, rescuing an administrator who has locked themselves out, and changing the support plan. Everyday work goes through the other door, I A M Identity Center. Alex signs in to one portal, and from it picks an account and a role. A role is a set of permissions that someone can step into for a while. In the development account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, the role is Book Shop Developer, and it may build and break things. In production, one one one one, two two two two, three three three three, the role is Book Shop Read Only: alex can look, and never touch. Two accounts, so that a mistake in development cannot reach the shop customers use. Next, we give the command line a way through that portal.

The project starts as a single file, a w s dash config, open in the editor. It holds the shop's profiles. A profile is a name the command line, the S D Ks and Terraform all understand. The highlighted one, book shop dev, says: sign in through the session called book shop, then use account four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, with the role Book Shop Developer, in the London Region, E U west two. Below it, book shop prod points at the production account with the read only role, and the last block describes the session both profiles share: the address of the access portal and the Region it lives in. In the terminal, we point the command line at this file with the variable A W S config file, and list profiles prints both names back. Then we ask A W S who we are with get caller identity, using the dev profile, and the command line refuses. The side pane shows why. The command line read the profile, found the session, and looked for a token from the portal, and there is none, because alex has never signed in. A token comes from a browser: alex signs in at the portal, the command line caches a token for some hours, and trades it for short lived credentials for the role. Without it, nothing was sent to A W S at all: this was not a denial, it was a request that never left the laptop. Signing in needs a real browser and a real A W S account. This course has neither, so next we put an emulator beside A W S.

The project gains a second file, env dot sh, open in the editor. Its first lines point every tool at the shop's profiles and at the London Region. The three highlighted lines are the emulator. A W S endpoint U R L sends every request to a server on this machine, port five thousand, instead of to A W S, and the two key lines are example credentials the emulator accepts. Nothing else changes: it is the real A W S command line, the real Python S D K, and later the real Terraform, just pointed somewhere else. The side pane shows the one choice that line makes. With the endpoint set, a request goes to localhost, to moto, the emulator. Without it, the same request goes to the S T S endpoint in E U west two, which is A W S itself. In the terminal we source the file and ask again who we are, and this time there is an answer: account four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, the development account, as a user the emulator calls moto. Then list buckets returns an empty list: a brand new account, with nothing in it yet. The table says what the emulator can and cannot show. It answers every A P I call, it keeps state, so what we create stays created, and when we switch it on, it evaluates I A M policies. It moves no packets, it cannot lose an Availability Zone, and it sends no bill: for those, the course uses small models and a rate card, and says so. Every terminal that talks to the emulator is labelled. Now, let's make the shop's first bucket.

The obvious way to make a bucket is a script, and the editor shows one: make bucket dot sh. Two highlighted commands, one A P I call each. Create bucket makes the catalog bucket, book shop catalog, followed by the account number, in London. Put bucket tagging labels it with app equals book shop. The line set dash e at the top stops the script at the first command that fails. In the terminal, the first run works: create bucket prints where the bucket is, and the script says it made it. Now run exactly the same script again, as anyone would, to be sure, or on a second laptop. Create bucket fails: bucket already owned by you. The side pane shows both runs. Run one made the bucket and tagged it. Run two failed on the bucket the first run made, and the tagging never ran at all. Nothing is broken, but the script cannot tell. It records what to do, one call after another, and has no idea what already exists. The table lists what that costs. Run it twice, and it fails on its own work. Let someone change the bucket in the console, and the script never knows. Want the bucket gone? That is another script. Review a change, and you are reading commands, not the result they will have. What we want instead is a file that says what should exist, and a tool that works out the calls. The last command removes the bucket, because in the next section Terraform makes it, and from then on Terraform owns it.

The script is gone. In its place is a folder called infra, and in the editor its first file, s three dot t f. It does not say create anything. It declares that a resource of type A W S S three bucket, called catalog, should exist, with this bucket name and the app tag. Beside it, providers dot t f pins Terraform and its A W S provider, the plugin that knows every A W S A P I. The terminal runs the three commands every later section runs. Terraform init downloads that provider, signed by HashiCorp, and writes a lock file that records exactly which version was used, so a teammate gets the same one. Terraform plan is the heart of it, and the side pane draws it. Plan compares three things: what the code says should exist, what Terraform's state says it made, and what is really in the account right now. The difference is the plan, here plus one bucket, and dash out saves exactly that plan to a file. Terraform apply, given the saved plan, can do nothing the plan did not show. It makes the create bucket call and writes the result into the state. Run plan again, and it would find nothing to do: the code, the state and the account agree. That is the difference from the script. Running it twice is safe, because Terraform starts from what exists. Init downloads and locks, plan compares and saves, apply makes it so and records it. But where exactly is that state, and what happens when someone changes the bucket behind Terraform's back?

Between the last section and this one, something happened that the project did not do. Sam, a teammate, opened the bucket in the A W S console and added a tag of their own: owner equals sam. The code in the editor did not change. In the terminal, terraform state list shows what Terraform believes it manages: one resource, the catalog bucket. Its state holds the bucket exactly as Terraform made it, with one tag. Then we ask the bucket itself for its tags, and it has two: app, and owner sam. The side pane lines up the three places a tag can be. The code says app equals book shop. The state says the same, because that is what Terraform made. The bucket has one more, and nobody told Terraform. This is drift: the real resource has moved away from the code. Terraform plan finds it. Before it compares anything, plan refreshes, reading every resource it manages from the account, and the refreshed bucket no longer matches the code. So the plan is an update in place, removing the owner tag. The table sums it up. Sam made the drift in the console. A plan noticed it, not the state on its own. And there are two cures: change the code to include the tag, if it belongs, or let apply put the bucket back. We will leave the plan unapplied for now. First, a bigger problem: that state is a file on alex's laptop, and sam has no way to see it.

A state file on one laptop is a problem the moment a second person, or a pipeline, runs Terraform. Each would plan against their own copy, and the second apply would overwrite the first. So the state moves into S three. That needs a bucket, and here is the chicken and the egg: the bucket that holds the state cannot keep its own state. So a separate root, infra slash bootstrap, makes it once, with local state: the bucket book shop t f state, versioning, so every write of the state is kept and a bad one can be rolled back, and a block on all public access. In the terminal, the bootstrap apply adds those three resources. Then the editor shows backend dot t f. It tells the main project to keep its state in that bucket, under the key book shop slash terraform dot t f state, and use lock file is the line that matters. Terraform init with migrate state copies the existing state up, and the backend is configured. Listing the bucket shows the state object, in the cloud now. The side pane shows what the lock file buys. Alex and the pipeline both run apply. Alex's run starts first and writes a lock object beside the state; the pipeline sees it and waits, instead of writing over alex's work. When alex's run finishes, the lock is removed and the pipeline goes ahead. The table at the bottom keeps the two roots straight: bootstrap's state is a local file, and everything else lives in the bucket bootstrap made. One more thing before the shop grows: knowing what it costs.

This is the book shop's map, the first time we see it. It is the whole finished shop, drawn the way A W S draws architecture: the Region, the network in the middle with its three Availability Zones, the services beside it, the account's controls along the bottom, and shoppers on the left. Almost everything is still greyed out, because the shop does not have it yet, but every part is already in the place it will have. What exists is in colour: the catalog bucket, the Terraform state bucket, and, new in this section and ringed, a budget. In the terminal, the plan does three things. It creates the budget: twenty U S dollars a month for development. It adds default tags to everything: app, the environment dev, and managed by terraform, so any resource in the bill can be traced back to this project. And it removes sam's owner tag, the drift from two sections ago, because the code still does not have it. Apply makes all three changes. The diagram under the terminal is the misconception to avoid. A budget is an alarm, not a cap. When the forecast spend for the month passes eighty percent of twenty dollars, alex gets an email, and that is all. A W S keeps serving, and keeps billing. The real way to stop paying is to remove what you no longer need, and terraform plan dash destroy shows exactly what that would be: the budget and the catalog bucket, two to destroy. The state bucket is not in the list, because bootstrap owns it. Cleaning up is one command, from the first resource on. Next course, the shop gets its first role, and we find out what a denied request looks like.

Every request A W S receives was made by someone, and before it does anything, A W S has to know who. That someone is called a principal, and the left of the frame lists the kinds. The root user, which we locked away in the last course. An I A M user, a long lived identity with a password or an access key. A person like alex, who signs in through Identity Center and works inside a role. And a service acting for us, like the container service E C S running the shop's code, which also works inside a role. In the middle is what each one signs its requests with. An I A M user's access key starts with A K I A and lasts until someone deletes it. A role session's credentials start with A S I A, come with a session token, and expire, after an hour by default. On the right is what A W S does with a request. Every request is signed with the secret half of a key. First comes authentication: is the signature right, and is the key real? Only then comes authorization: do the policies allow this principal to take this action on this resource? The table makes the case for roles. If a long term key leaks, it works until someone notices. If temporary credentials leak, they stop working on their own. So the book shop uses no long term keys at all: alex works through a role, the app will work through a role, and later so will the delivery pipeline. Next, the app gets its role.

The project gains a file, i a m dot t f, open in the editor. It declares the app's identity: a role called Book Shop App. A role has no password and no key of its own; it is a set of permissions that a trusted principal can step into for a while. The highlighted lines are its trust policy, and they answer one question: who may become this role? Here, one principal: the service E C S tasks dot amazonaws dot com, which is how the container service runs the shop's code in Course 6. In the terminal, plan and apply create the role. Then we read it back from the emulator. Get role shows the trust policy as A W S stored it: allow, the service E C S tasks, the action S T S assume role. List role policies shows the other half, and it is empty. The side pane draws the two questions a role answers. The arrow from E C S into the role is trust: who may assume it. The arrow out of the role is permissions: what it may do, and it is dashed, because so far the answer is nothing. The table keeps them apart. A trust policy names a principal, and a role has exactly one. A permissions policy names actions and resources, and a role can have any number. With none at all, a role is allowed to do nothing, so Book Shop App is denied everything. Next, we become the role, and see that for ourselves.

From this section on, the emulator checks every request against I A M, with one exception it says out loud: alex's own requests stand for alex's developer role, which may do anything in development. Alex starts by uploading the shop's first book page, bk one zero zero one, into the catalog bucket. Then alex asks S T S, the security token service, to assume the app's role. On A W S, only E C S could do this, because the trust policy names only E C S. The emulator does not hold alex to the trust policy, so here alex stands in for E C S, and the frame says so. The answer is a set of temporary credentials: a key starting with A S I A, a secret, a session token, and an expiry one hour from now. The editor shows the small tool that does this for us: as app dot s h asks for those credentials, puts them in the environment, and runs one command with them. Asked who it is, the tool's command answers: the assumed role Book Shop App, session task one. Then, as the app, it tries to read the very book alex just uploaded, and S three says no: forbidden, a four oh three, on its very first request, which asks for the object's details. The side pane follows the steps: the caller asks S T S for the role, gets credentials, and signs the request with them, and that request is refused. The table shows the point: the same read, alex allowed, the app refused. A role with no permissions policy can do nothing, and that is the right place to start. Next, we give it exactly one thing it may do.

The editor shows the role's first permissions policy, written with a Terraform data source that builds the J S O N for us. It has one statement, highlighted, and every statement has the same parts. A statement I D, read books, so we can talk about it. The effect, allow. The action, S three get object, written as service colon operation. And the resource it applies to, as an A R N: the catalog bucket's A R N, slash books, slash star. The star matches any key under books, and nothing else. The side pane takes the statement apart: effect, action, resource, and a fourth, optional part, a condition, which this statement does not use. In the terminal, plan shows the policy being added to the role, inline, and apply adds it. Then the app tries three things. Reading bk one zero zero one now works, and the book's J S O N comes back. Reading orders dot c s v is refused with a four oh three: the action matches, but the resource is not under books. And writing a new book is refused: the resource matches, but the action is put object, not get object. The table lines the three up. A statement allows a request only when every one of its parts matches, and anything nothing allowed is denied. That is the whole idea of least privilege: start from nothing, and allow exactly what the shop needs. Next, the full picture of how A W S reaches a decision.

This is the chart A W S uses to decide every request inside one account, and it is worth knowing by heart. A request starts denied. First, A W S reads every policy that applies, looking for an explicit deny. If any statement anywhere says deny and matches, the answer is deny, and nothing can override it. Otherwise, if the account belongs to an organization, its guardrails must allow the request, or it is denied. Then, if a resource policy, like a bucket policy, allows it, the request is allowed. If not, an identity policy, like the role's own, must allow it, and if one is set, a permissions boundary and the session's policy must agree. If nothing allowed it, that is an implicit deny. On the right is a small lab, run against the emulator with I A M checks on. The role's policy has two statements: read books allows get object on books, and no drafts denies get object on books slash drafts. The lab then makes three requests as the role. Reading bk one zero zero one is allowed. Reading a draft is denied, even though read books matches it too, because no drafts is an explicit deny, and an explicit deny always wins. Writing bk one zero zero two is denied too, but for a different reason: no statement allows put object, so it falls all the way through to an implicit deny. The outcomes are the emulator's; the table reads, from the policy, where on the chart each request stopped. Next, we meet an implicit deny in the shop itself, and fix it.

The shop's home page will list every book, so the app needs to list the catalog. In the terminal, the app lists books slash in the bucket, and is refused: access denied, when calling list objects. Why, when the role may read every book? The side pane shows what I A M compared. Listing is the action S three list bucket, and its resource is the bucket itself, not the objects inside it. Read books names objects, books slash star, so it does not match, nothing else allows the request, and that is an implicit deny. This is the most common mistake in S three policies: putting slash star on list bucket, which then matches nothing. The fix is already in the editor, highlighted: a second statement, list books, allowing list bucket, with the bucket's own A R N as its resource. The table at the bottom of the side pane is the rule to remember: get object and put object act on a bucket slash a key; list bucket acts on the bucket. Terraform plan shows the change as an update in place to the role's inline policy, with the new statement added to its J S O N. Apply makes it. The app lists books slash again, and this time the bucket answers: one book, bk one zero zero one dot json. A denial is not a failure of I A M; it is I A M working. Read which action was refused, find its resource, and allow exactly that. Next, a policy of a different kind, attached to the bucket, and a second account.

So far every policy has been attached to the one asking, the role. This section attaches one to the thing being asked for: the catalog bucket. That is a resource policy, and the editor shows it, in s three dot t f. The highlighted lines are what makes it different: a principal. A resource policy always says who it is talking to. This one lets the Auditor role, in the company's audit account, seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine, get objects from the catalog and list it. In the terminal, plan and apply put the policy on the bucket, and get bucket policy reads it back, exactly as stored. The side pane shows the two accounts. On the right, the shop's development account, with the bucket and its new policy. On the left, the audit account, with the Auditor role and its own identity policy. That identity policy is not ours to write; the audit account's administrators own it. The rule the arrow carries is the one to remember: across accounts, both sides must allow. The bucket policy alone is not enough, and neither is the auditor's own policy. Within one account, as the table shows, either one allowing is enough. One honest note, in red: the emulator stores and returns this policy, but it does not evaluate resource policies or a second account, so that rule comes from A W S's documentation, not from a run. Next, the accounts themselves, and the guardrails above them.

The book shop now has several accounts: development, production, and the auditors' account. A W S Organizations ties them into one tree, managed from one more account, the management account, one two three four five six seven eight nine zero one two, which pays the bills and runs the organization, and runs nothing else. On the left is the tree. Under the root are organizational units, folders for accounts. Security holds the audit account. Workloads holds two more: Prod, with the production account, and Dev, with the development account where the shop is built. The terminal on the right is a lab: a separate Terraform root, applied to the emulator from the management account, that creates exactly these units and a policy. Listing the root's units prints Security and Workloads. Listing the policies on Workloads prints two: Full A W S Access, which A W S attaches everywhere by default and which allows everything, and London Only. London Only is a service control policy. It denies every action outside E U west two, except for global services like I A M, and it is attached to Workloads, so it reaches Prod and Dev, but not Security. The table spells that out, including the management account, which service control policies never restrict. The diagram underneath is the misconception to avoid. A service control policy grants nothing. It is a ceiling: the most any role in those accounts may do. What a role can actually do is only what both its own policies and the ceiling allow. The emulator creates these units and stores the policy, but does not enforce it, and the frame says so. That completes the shop's identities and guardrails. Next course, it gets a network.

Before the book shop gets a network, it needs a plan for its addresses, and this frame is that plan. Start on the left with the notation. Ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen means: the first sixteen bits, ten dot twenty, are fixed, and the last sixteen are free for hosts. Two to the power of thirty two minus sixteen is sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six addresses. A slash twenty four fixes twenty four bits, and leaves two hundred and fifty six. Under the table is the real output of a small Python program, the address plan run locally with Python's own I P address module. In the middle is that plan as a picture. The V P C, the shop's private network, takes the whole slash sixteen. It is carved into nine slash twenty fours: three tiers, each in three Availability Zones. The public tier, ten dot twenty dot zero to two, faces the internet: the load balancer and the N A T gateways will live there. The app tier, ten dot twenty dot ten to twelve, holds the shop's tasks. The data tier, ten dot twenty dot twenty to twenty two, holds the database. The gaps between ten and twenty leave room for each tier to grow, and below them, the rest of the range is free: room for two hundred and thirty three more subnets. Only three and a half percent is used. On the right, we open up one subnet, public c. Of its two hundred and fifty six addresses, A W S keeps five: the network address, the V P C router, the D N S resolver, one reserved for later, and the broadcast address. Two hundred and fifty one are left for the shop. Next, we build this V P C in Terraform.

Back on the map, the network appears. The V P C is the shop's private network in E U west two, and inside it, coloured in now, are its nine subnets: in each of the three Availability Zones, a public one, an app one and a data one. The code is on the right, in network dot t f, and it does not list nine subnets. A locals block builds them from the address plan of the last section: for each tier, public, app and data, and for each zone, a, b and c, a name like app dash b, its zone, and its slash twenty four, ten dot twenty dot eleven dot zero. Then one resource block, A W S subnet, with for each over that map, makes all nine, each tagged with its name and tier. Change the plan, and the subnets follow. Apply creates ten resources: the V P C and the nine subnets. The query under it reads them back from the account, filtered to this V P C by its id, which Terraform gives us as an output, because the account has a second V P C we did not make: every A W S account starts with a default V P C in each Region, ready for quick experiments. The shop does not use it. Notice what this network can do so far: nothing reaches it from outside, and nothing in it reaches out. Subnets are places to put things; where packets may go is decided by route tables, and that is next.

Every subnet answers to exactly one route table, and routes dot t f creates two. The public table will serve the three public subnets; the private table serves the other six, the app and the data tiers. The association block at the bottom ties each subnet to its table, with the same for each over the subnets, choosing by tier. A new table already holds one route that nobody wrote: ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen to local. It means that inside the V P C, every subnet can reach every other. That is all the network can do right now. To see it, the project gains a small tool, which route dot p y. It reads the real route tables from the account, finds the table a subnet answers to, and picks a route the way the V P C router does: of all the routes whose destination contains the address, the most specific one, the longest prefix, wins. The router itself and the packets are not emulated, so the tool is how we look. From app a, the address ten dot twenty dot twenty dot fifteen, in data a, matches the local route, and goes there. From public a, one nine eight dot fifty one dot one hundred dot seven, a payments service on the internet, matches nothing at all: the packet is dropped. The side pane puts it together: nine subnets, two tables, each holding only local. A brand new V P C is an island. Every way in or out is a route that someone adds on purpose, and the first one is the way in.

The way in is an internet gateway, added at the bottom of routes dot t f. There is one per V P C, and A W S runs it across every zone, so it is not a single point of failure. On its own it does nothing. The second block is what matters: a route in the public table only, sending zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, which means every address, to the gateway. Because the local route is more specific, traffic inside the V P C still stays inside; everything else from a public subnet now goes out through the gateway, and replies come back the same way. The tool shows it. From public a, the payments address now matches two routes, local does not contain it, and zero slash zero does, so it goes to the internet gateway. From app a, nothing has changed: its private table still has only local, and the packet is dropped. The side pane draws the two tables side by side: the public one with a door, the private one with none. And this is the definition worth remembering. A subnet is public because its route table sends zero slash zero to an internet gateway. Nothing else makes it public: the word public in its name is only a label we chose. The load balancer will live in these subnets, reachable from the internet. The shop's tasks will not. But they still need to reach out, to call the payments service, and that needs a different kind of door.

On the map, a N A T gateway appears in the public subnet of zone a. N A T stands for network address translation. It is the way out for private subnets: the private route table now sends zero slash zero to it, and it forwards the traffic through the internet gateway, rewriting the source address to its own public one. In the terminal, the tool shows the new route: from app a, the payments address now goes to the N A T gateway. And from data b, an address in the app tier still goes local, because local is more specific than zero slash zero. The diagram under the terminal is the point of this section: who may start a connection. A task in app a may start one, out through the N A T, to the internet, and the reply comes back to it. Nothing on the internet can start a connection to the task: there is no route in, and the N A T only answers connections that came from inside. Out, but never in. One decision is worth saying aloud. Development runs one N A T gateway, in zone a, because each one costs money every hour it exists and for every gigabyte it processes. The price of saving is resilience: if zone a fails, the private subnets in all three zones lose the internet. Production will run one per zone. Routes decide where packets may go. Next, firewalls decide who may connect at all.

Routes say where a packet can go; firewalls say whether it may arrive. Security dot t f creates three security groups, one per role: alb for the load balancer, app for the shop's tasks, and db for the orders database. A security group sits on each network interface, and its inbound rules say who may start a connection in. The highlighted rules are the chain. Anyone may connect to the alb group on four four three and eighty. The app group accepts port eighty eighty, but only from the alb group: not from an address range, from a group, so whatever is behind the load balancer, however many tasks, the rule never changes. The db group accepts five four three two, only from the app group. The tool reads the rules back from the account, by group name, and prints exactly that chain, drawn in the side pane: anyone to alb, alb to app, app to db. Nothing else can reach the database at all. Security groups are stateful: a reply to a connection that was allowed in is always let back out. The file ends with the other kind of firewall, a network A C L, on the three data subnets. The table compares them. A security group is on an interface and only allows. A network A C L is on a subnet, it can allow and deny, its rules are checked in order, and it is stateless: it sees every packet alone, so the reply needs its own rule, which is why it has an outbound rule for the app tier's high ports. Next, all of it together, in one request.

Here is everything this course builds, used by one page view. A shopper's browser asks for book shop dot example dot com slash books slash b k one thousand and one. Step one is the name. The browser asks the D N S, and Route fifty three answers with the addresses of the load balancer. That is the first edge, a question and its answer. Step two, the browser connects to one of those addresses on port four four three. The packet arrives at the internet gateway, and the public route table carries it into the public subnet. Step three, it reaches the load balancer's network interface, where the alb security group decides: four four three, from anyone, allowed. Step four is T L S. The load balancer presents its certificate, which proves it really is book shop dot example dot com, and the encrypted request is decrypted here. Step five, the load balancer picks a task that its health checks say is healthy, and sends the request on, as plain H T T P, to port eighty eighty in an app subnet. Step six, the task's interface asks the app security group, which allows eighty eighty from the alb group. The task is greyed: it arrives in Course Six. Step seven, the reply goes back the same way, with no rule needed, because security groups are stateful. The table on the bottom names who decides at each hop, and the section that builds it. Two pieces are still missing: the load balancer, and the name and certificate. They come next.

The load balancer appears on the map, spanning the three public subnets: one name, with a node in every zone, so losing a zone does not lose the front door. Its security group is alb. Behind it, a target group says where requests go: port eighty eighty, by I P address, which is how Fargate tasks will register in Course Six, and a listener on port eighty forwards to it for now. In the terminal, the account reports the load balancer: its D N S name, internet facing, and active. Then the target group's health: an empty list, because there are no targets yet. The diagram under the terminal is how the load balancer decides who gets traffic, using this shop's own settings. Every ten seconds it asks each target for slash health. A new target starts as initial. Three passes in a row, and it is healthy and gets requests. Two failures in a row, and it is unhealthy and gets none, so a broken task stops receiving shoppers within about twenty seconds, without anyone being paged. When a target is removed, say during a deploy, it drains for thirty seconds, finishing the requests it already has before it goes. The emulator records these settings but does not run checks, so the timings come from the A W S documentation, not from a run. The load balancer now answers plain H T T P on its own long name. Shoppers need the shop's name, and a padlock.

D N S dot t f gives the shop its name. A Route fifty three hosted zone holds the records for book shop dot example dot com. Outside A W S, the domain's registrar points the domain at the zone's four name servers; that step is described, not emulated. Next, a certificate from A C M, the certificate manager, validated by D N S: A C M asks for one special record to prove we control the name, Terraform writes it into the zone, and the certificate is issued. The highlighted block is the name itself: an alias A record pointing at the load balancer. An alias, not a plain address, because the load balancer's addresses change; Route fifty three follows them. Alb dot t f changed too: an H T T P S listener on four four three, with the certificate and a modern T L S policy, and the port eighty listener now only answers: go to H T T P S. The plan shows it: six to add, one to change. Reading back, the zone holds the alias record and the validation record A C M asked for, beside the name server records every zone has; the listeners are eighty, redirect, and four four three, forward. The side pane draws both halves. Finding the name: the shopper's resolver walks from dot com to example dot com, which delegates to Route fifty three's name servers, and the hosted zone answers with the alias. And where encryption ends: H T T P S from the browser to the load balancer, then plain H T T P inside the V P C to the task. Encrypting that last hop too is a choice, and the next section saves money instead.

The shop's tasks will read every book page from the catalog bucket in S three. Right now, that traffic would leave the private subnet through the N A T gateway and the internet gateway, and the N A T gateway charges for every gigabyte it processes. Endpoint dot t f fixes that with a gateway endpoint for S three. It adds one route to the private table: S three's address ranges, held by A W S as a prefix list, to the endpoint. The terminal reads the prefix list from the account, and the tool picks a route for one of its addresses from app a. Two routes match now: zero slash zero to the N A T, and the prefix list to the endpoint. The prefix list is more specific, so it wins, and the request never touches the N A T gateway. The side pane draws both paths: before, task to N A T to internet gateway to S three, dashed; now, task to the endpoint to S three. A gateway endpoint for S three has no hourly charge and no per gigabyte charge, and the traffic stays on A W S's network. The route table at the bottom shows the new row, ringed. That completes the shop's network: an address plan, nine subnets in three zones, doors in and out, firewalls in a chain, a load balancer with health checks, a name with a certificate, and a private path to S three. All of it is still empty. In the next course, the shop's own code moves in.

The shop has a network, a role and a catalog, but nothing serves a page yet. This section adds the app itself, a small Python package called book shop. The editor shows web dot p y. It is an H T T P server from Python's own standard library, so the app needs only one package beyond Python, boto three, to talk to A W S. The highlighted handler answers two paths. Slash health answers status ok: that is what the load balancer will check. Slash books slash an I D asks catalog dot p y for the book, and catalog dot p y reads the page from the catalog bucket with one S three get object call. Anything else is a four oh four. In the terminal we start the app in the background, on port eight zero eight zero, and ask it three things. Health says ok. Book one zero zero one comes back as the J S O N page we uploaded in Course 4, read from the emulated bucket. And a book that does not exist answers no such book, with a four oh four. Then we stop the app and read its log: one line of J S O N per request, with the path and the status, written to standard output. The side pane follows one request through the code: curl, the handler, the catalog module, the bucket. The app keeps nothing of its own: the books live in S three, so any number of copies of it can answer the same way. Next, tests that check all this without A W S, and without the emulator.

The project gains a tests folder, and the editor shows its shared fixture, conftest dot p y. Every test that needs A W S asks for this fixture, and the highlighted lines are the point. It removes the emulator's endpoint, and it sets fake keys. Then mock A W S, from the moto library, takes over boto three inside the test process itself, and the fixture creates the catalog bucket and one book in it. If a call ever escaped the mock, it would have nowhere to go and fake keys to sign with, so it would fail, never reach a real account. The side pane draws the path. A test calls the app's code, unchanged; the code calls boto three, the real client; and boto three's request is intercepted in memory, before it leaves the process. In the terminal, pytest runs five tests. Two call the catalog module directly: one reads a book, one asks for a missing book and expects not found. Three start the real H T T P server on a free port and ask it for health, a book, and an unknown book. All five pass, in a couple of seconds. The table keeps the two tools apart. The emulator is a server that keeps its state between commands, which is what this course's terminal needs. The mock lives inside one test and starts empty every time, which is what tests need: no order between them, nothing left behind. Next, before we package the app, a step back: which of A W S's ways to run code should run it?

A W S runs code in many ways, and the four that matter for a web service are on screen. Each column is the same stack of five layers: your code, its packaging, how many copies run and where, the operating system and its patches, and the hardware. Orange is yours, blue is A W S's. On E C two, you rent a virtual server: the hardware is A W S's, and everything above it is yours, including patching the operating system and deciding how many servers to run. On E C S with Fargate, you hand A W S a container image and say how many copies you want; the servers, their operating system and their capacity are A W S's. On Lambda, you hand over only your code, and A W S runs it when an event arrives, as many copies as the events need. And E K S is managed Kubernetes: the Kubernetes control plane is A W S's, but the nodes it runs on, and their operating system, are yours unless you add Fargate there too. The table says when each one fits. E C two, when you need the server itself. Fargate, for a long running web service in containers with no servers to look after: that is the book shop, and it is the course's choice. Lambda, for short pieces of work triggered by events: the shop will use one for fulfilment in Course 8. And E K S, when a team already runs Kubernetes and many services on it. In section nine we will plan the same app on E C two, to see exactly what Fargate takes off our hands. First, the app needs to become an image.

Fargate runs containers, so the app becomes a container image. The editor shows the Dockerfile. It starts from the official Python three point one three slim image, pinned by its digest, so every build starts from exactly the same bytes. It copies requirements dot t x t and installs it: a lock file that pins boto three and every package boto three pulls in, so nothing floats between two builds. Only then does it copy the app's code, so a change to the code rebuilds one small layer, not the dependencies. It runs as the user nobody, and its command starts the web server. In the terminal, Terraform first makes the registry: an E C R repository called book shop, whose tags can never move, so one point zero point zero always means the same image. Then a real docker build, and docker history lists what the side pane draws: the image is a stack of layers, Debian, Python, the locked packages, and on top, the app itself, a few kilobytes. We run the image as a container against the emulator, and it serves book one zero zero one, exactly as the app did on its own. The image freezes the operating system, Python, every package and the code. What it does not freeze is configuration: which bucket comes from an environment variable, credentials come from the role, and the data stays in S three. Last, the push. The emulator speaks E C R's A P I but not the registry protocol, so the tool registers the image's manifest, the document docker push sends last, and E C R now lists one point zero point zero, with the same digest the build printed. The frame says so. Next, a definition of how to run it.

A task definition is the recipe for running one copy of the shop, and the editor shows it, in task dot t f. It names the image in E C R, half a virtual C P U and one gigabyte of memory, port eight zero eight zero, the catalog bucket as an environment variable, and a log group for the container's output. The highlighted lines are the part people mix up: two roles. The execution role belongs to E C S, not to the app. E C S uses it before and around the app: to pull the image from E C R and to send the container's output to the log group. Its policy, above in the same file, allows exactly that: pull from this repository, write to this log group. The task role is the app's own, Book Shop App, from Course 4. The app's code signs its requests with it, so reading a book from the catalog uses the task role and nothing else. In the terminal, plan and apply create the log group, the execution role and its policy, and the task definition, revision one. Reading it back from the emulator shows both roles, by A R N. The side pane draws the split, and the table goes moment by moment: pulling the image, E C S with the execution role; creating the log stream, E C S with the execution role; reading book one zero zero one, the app with the task role. Keep them apart, and a leaked app credential can never pull images or write other logs. Next, something that runs this definition, and keeps it running.

Back on the shop's map. In this section the three app tasks appear, one in each app subnet, ringed, and with them, now in colour, the image registry and the logs along the bottom. The terminal shows the plan for two resources. A cluster, called book shop, which is just a name to group services under. And a service: run the task definition with a desired count of three, on Fargate, in the three app subnets, behind the app security group, and register every task in the load balancer's target group on port eight zero eight zero. The diagram under the terminal says what a service is for: it keeps three tasks alive. If a task stops, or fails its health checks, E C S starts another one to get back to three, and every new task registers itself with the target group, where the health checks from Course 5 decide when it gets traffic. Now the honest part, in red. The emulator records the service exactly as declared, desired three, launch type Fargate, but it runs no containers: running count zero, and no tasks. On A W S, E C S would now start three tasks from the image in E C R, one per Availability Zone, so losing a zone loses a third of the shop, not all of it. What we can check here is the declaration, and it is right. Next, how three becomes more when the evening comes.

Three tasks is a floor, not a plan for the evening. The editor shows scaling dot t f. A scalable target lets the service's desired count move between three and twelve: three so there is always one per Availability Zone, twelve as a ceiling on cost. And a target tracking policy, highlighted: keep the service's average C P U at sixty percent. Add tasks quickly, at most once a minute; remove them slowly, five minutes apart, so a short dip does not throw away capacity the next minute needs. The terminal reads both back from the emulator: minimum three, maximum twelve, target sixty, and the two cooldowns. The side pane is what the policy does, from a small model, labelled as one. Once a minute, CloudWatch measures the average C P U. When it stays above sixty for three minutes, an alarm fires, and the policy sets the desired count in proportion: tasks times C P U, divided by sixty. In the model, traffic climbs from one hundred and twenty to four hundred and twenty requests a second between quarter to six and six. With three tasks, C P U passes sixty and keeps climbing, up to eighty seven percent, because the alarm needs three minutes and a new task needs two more to start. Then the service catches up, four, five, six, seven tasks, and C P U settles back on its target. The lesson is the lag: scaling reacts in minutes, so the target leaves headroom for the minutes it takes. Next, what happens to a task when the evening ends and it is taken away.

Tasks are removed all the time: when the evening ends, on every deploy, when one fails a health check. So a task must keep nothing it needs, and the shop's tasks keep nothing: the catalog is in S three. And it must stop cleanly. The side pane shows the order in which E C S removes a task. First the load balancer drains it: no new requests, and thirty seconds for those in flight. Then E C S sends the container the signal SIGTERM. If it is still running thirty seconds later, the stop timeout, SIGKILL ends it. By default, Python dies the moment SIGTERM arrives, and a request in progress dies with it. The editor shows the fix in web dot p y, highlighted: on SIGTERM, log it, stop accepting new connections, let the requests already accepted finish, and exit. The terminal proves it with a small tool, drain dot p y. It starts the app, sends half a request, sends SIGTERM, then sends the rest. The request still finishes with two hundred, O K, and the app exits with zero; its own output shows stopping, the request, and stopped cleanly. Then the new version ships the way every change will. Build book shop one point one point zero, push it, change the task definition to the new tag, and apply: a new revision, revision two, and the service now runs it. On A W S, E C S would replace the tasks one by one, each one draining before it stops. Next, the same app on E C two, to see what Fargate has been doing for us.

To see what Fargate does for the shop, here is the same app on E C two, side by side. On the left, the shop as it is: one service keeping three tasks, half a virtual C P U each, and the servers, their operating system and their patches belong to A W S. On the right, what E C two would need, written as Terraform in a separate root and planned against the emulator, never applied to the shop. An Auto Scaling group, three to twelve servers across the three Availability Zones. A launch template that every server starts from: an instance type, t three small, and user data, a start up script that installs Docker and runs the very same image. And an Amazon machine image, Amazon Linux, which A W S publishes but which is now ours to keep current. The terminal shows the plan: two resources to add, the group and the template. The table lists what moves to you. The operating system and its patches: on Fargate, A W S's; on E C two, yours, by building a new image and rolling it through the group. Size: Fargate sizes each task, E C two sizes whole servers, and packing tasks onto them is your job. Scaling: tasks on Fargate; on E C two, servers and the tasks on them. And the bill: Fargate charges for what tasks ask for, E C two for whole servers, busy or idle. E C two still wins when you need the server itself. For a web shop, Fargate is less to run. That completes Course 6: the shop runs. Next course, it keeps its data.

The shop has a few kinds of data now, and more are coming: book pages, review photos, orders, carts, stock counts. A W S has a store for each kind, and the first question splits them. Is it a file, or is it a record? Files and blobs go left. S three keeps whole objects by key, and that is where the book pages are, and where review photos will go. E B S is a disk for one server, and E F S is a file system many servers share; the shop uses neither, because its Fargate tasks keep nothing on disk. Records go right, and here the question is how they are used. An order is several rows that must change together or not at all, and the finance team will ask questions of them in S Q L, so orders go to a relational database, R D S running PostgreSQL. A cart or a stock count is read and written by its key, very often, by any number of tasks, so those go to DynamoDB, a key value store that scales without a server to size. And the same book page, read thousands of times an evening, can be kept in memory in front of S three, in ElastiCache, accepting that the copy can be a little out of date. The table gives each need its reason. The rest of this course builds every one of these, in order: the catalog bucket, uploads, the orders database and its password, carts, the last copy in stock, and a cache.

The catalog bucket has held book pages since Course 4, with no protection against a bad edit. The editor shows three additions to s three dot t f. Versioning: every write now keeps the page it replaced, so a mistake is undone by restoring the version before it, and a delete only hides an object. A lifecycle rule: an old version lives thirty days and is then deleted, so the bucket keeps history, not everything forever. And, in the bucket policy, a statement called https only: deny every action, to everyone, when the request did not arrive over H T T P S. In the terminal, apply makes the changes. Then the price of book one zero zero one changes, from twelve ninety nine to ten ninety nine, and we upload the new page. Listing the object's versions shows two. The latest, with a version I D, is the new page. The older one has the version I D null, because it was written before versioning was turned on. The side pane draws it: one key that readers ask for, two versions behind it, and the older one on its way out after thirty days. One honest note about the policy. The emulator listens on plain H T T P, but every request it stands in for is H T T P S on A W S, so it evaluates the policy as A W S would see those requests. That a plain H T T P request is refused is A W S's documentation, not something this run shows. Next, a bucket that shoppers write to, without ever holding a credential.

Shoppers will attach a photo to a review. The photo should go straight from the browser to S three, without passing through the app, and the browser must never hold an A W S credential. The answer is a presigned U R L, and the editor shows the whole of it, uploads dot p y. The app asks boto three to sign a put object request for one key, reviews slash the book slash the review dot j p g, of type image j p e g, valid for three hundred seconds. Signing happens on the app's side, with the app's own permissions, and the role in i a m dot t f may sign uploads only under reviews. In the terminal, Terraform makes the uploads bucket: private, all public access blocked, and a cors rule that lets the shop's own pages, and only those, send a put. The app is started and asked for a U R L. The answer is the key, the expiry, and the U R L itself: the S three address, with the signature, the credential's I D and the expiry in its query string. Then curl, which holds no A W S credentials at all, puts the photo to that U R L, and the bucket answers two hundred. Listing the bucket shows the photo, six hundred and seventy six bytes, under reviews. The side pane numbers the steps: the browser asks the app, the app signs, the browser uploads. The table says exactly what the U R L allows: one method, one key, one content type, five minutes, and only what the signer may do. Next, the database for orders.

Back on the map, the data subnets get their first tenant. The orders database appears in eu west two a, ringed, with its standby beside it in two b, and the secret that holds its password lights up along the bottom. The terminal shows the plan for an R D S instance: PostgreSQL sixteen point nine, the smallest instance class that runs in two zones, twenty gigabytes of encrypted storage, backups kept for seven days, in the data subnets, behind the database security group from Course 5. Two choices matter most. Multi A Z is on: R D S keeps a standby copy in a second Availability Zone and writes every change to it before the change commits, so if the primary's zone fails, the same name points at the standby within a minute or two, and no committed order is lost. The standby takes no reads; it exists to take over. And manage master user password is on: nobody chooses the password, R D S generates it and keeps it in Secrets Manager. Reading the instance back from the emulator shows Multi A Z true, the primary in eu west two a, the standby in eu west two b, the endpoint's name, and the A R N of that secret. The red note is the honest part. The emulator records the instance, its zones and its secret, but it runs no database. The S Q L in the next section runs in a real PostgreSQL sixteen on this machine, standing in for the one R D S would run. Next, placing an order, in one transaction.

An order touches several rows: the order itself, a line for each book, and the stock of each book. They must change together, or not at all, and that is what a transaction is for. The schema, in the migrations folder, has one rule that matters here: a book's stock must be zero or more, a check the database enforces itself. The editor shows place order, in orders dot p y. Inside one transaction, it reads the prices, inserts the order and gets its number back, then for each book inserts a line and takes the copies out of stock. In the terminal, we create the database, run the migration, which adds two books, and place two orders. Customer c seventeen buys two copies of book one zero zero one: order one, twenty one pounds ninety eight. Customer c eighteen asks for one copy of one zero zero one and two of one zero zero two, which has a single copy left. The side pane follows that second order. The transaction begins, the order and its first line are written, and one copy of one zero zero one is taken. Then two copies of one zero zero two would leave minus one, the check fails, and PostgreSQL rolls back everything the transaction did. The table proves it: there is still only one order, and one zero zero one's stock is thirty eight, not thirty seven, because the copy taken a moment earlier was given back. Nothing half done, no stock lost. This is real PostgreSQL output, not the emulator. Next, how the app gets the database password, without anyone handing it over.

The orders database has a password that no person chose and nobody should copy. R D S keeps it in Secrets Manager and can rotate it. So the app must read it at the moment it connects, and the editor shows how, in orders dot p y. Connect looks for D B secret A R N. On A W S, the task gets that A R N and the database's address as environment variables, neither of them secret, and fetches the user and password from Secrets Manager with its role, then connects over T L S. On this machine, without that variable, it falls back to the local database. In i a m dot t f, the role gets one new statement, read database secret, for exactly one A R N: that secret. Terraform also creates a second secret, for the payment provider's A P I key in Course 8, and only the secret: its value will be set by hand, so it never sits in Terraform's state or in git. In the terminal, acting as the app, we read the database secret. The username is shop, and the password, which we print only the length of, is twenty eight characters. Then, still as the app, we try the payments key, and are refused: access denied. Under the emulator's I A M checks, the role reads the one secret it was given, and nothing else. The side pane follows the password at connect time: the code, the role, the secret, the database. Nothing about it is in the image, in the task definition, or in git. Next, carts, in a very different kind of database.

A cart is read and written constantly, always by its owner's key, and it does not need S Q L. So carts go to DynamoDB, a table with no server to size, billed per request. The table's design is the key. The partition key is the customer, and the sort key is the book. Every book in one customer's cart therefore shares a partition key, and DynamoDB keeps them together, sorted by book, as one item collection. The editor shows cart dot p y. Add uses an update with add quantity, so adding the same book twice changes one item instead of making two, and it pushes the expiry thirty days out, for the table's time to live. Contents reads the whole cart with a single query on the customer's key. In the terminal, Terraform makes the table, on demand, with time to live on the expires attribute, and the role is allowed to query and update it. Then two shoppers fill their carts. Customer c seventeen adds two copies of one zero zero one and one of one zero zero two, then one zero zero one again, and the cart now holds three. A scan of the table shows three items. The side pane draws them as DynamoDB stores them: one item collection per customer, c seventeen with two books, c eighteen with one. And reading a cart is always the same three steps: the customer's key, hashed to one partition, and one query that returns every book in order. No join, no scan, at any number of shoppers. Next, two of those shoppers want the last copy of a book.

Both shoppers now have the same cart, three copies of book one zero zero one and one of one zero zero two, and there is one copy of one zero zero two left. A stock table now holds a count per book, and checkout, in stock dot p y, does two things in one DynamoDB transaction. For every book in the cart, it takes the copies out of stock, on a condition, highlighted: stock must be at least the number asked for. And it deletes the cart's items. Either all of it happens, or none of it. In the terminal, a small tool sets the stock, thirty eight and one, and starts both checkouts at the same moment, two threads released together. One transaction commits: that shopper bought both books. The other is cancelled, because when it came to check, the condition stock at least one was false. The scans prove what that means. Book one zero zero two's stock is zero, never minus one. Book one zero zero one's stock is thirty five: the winner's three copies were taken, and the loser's three were not, because a cancelled transaction takes nothing. And the losing shopper's cart is still there, both books in it, ready for another try. The side pane shows the race, and which shopper won is whatever the two threads did, read from this run. The table says why only one can win. The condition is checked and written in one step for each item, the transaction covers every item of a checkout, and no lock is ever held, so the loser does not wait, it fails at once and can try again. Next, a cache in front of the book pages.

In the evening, the same book pages are read thousands of times, and each read goes to S three. A cache keeps a copy in memory, close to the app. On the left is the pattern the shop would use, cache aside. To read a page, the app tries the cache. On a hit, it answers from memory. On a miss, it reads the catalog, and keeps the page in the cache for sixty seconds. To change a page, the app writes the catalog, and then deletes the cached copy, so the next read is a miss and fetches the new one. Below, Terraform plans the cache itself: ElastiCache running Valkey, the open source Redis, a primary and a replica in two zones, encrypted in transit. It is planned, not applied: the emulator cannot run ElastiCache's replication groups, and the frame says so. On the right is a simulation, with a dictionary for the cache and a clock we step, of the price change from earlier in this course. At ten seconds, book one zero zero one drops from twelve ninety nine to ten ninety nine. With a time to live alone, the cache keeps serving the old price until the copy expires: stale from ten seconds to fifty nine. When the write also deletes the cached page, the very next read is a miss, and every read after it shows ten ninety nine. The table sums up the trade: deleting on write costs one call per change and removes the stale window, and a time to live is still worth keeping, to bound the damage when a delete is missed. That completes Course 7: the shop keeps its data. Next course, its checkout stops waiting.

So far, everything the shop does happens while the shopper waits. This course changes that, and the frame shows why, with the same checkout drawn twice. Above, as one request. Checkout records the order, then calls the payment provider, then the warehouse, then the loyalty service, one after another, and the shopper waits for all of it. The wait is the sum of every step. Worse, if the warehouse is down, the checkout fails, although the order itself was fine. And on a busy evening, every one of those services has to take the peak at the same moment. Below, the same checkout as events. Checkout records the order, which is the one thing it must wait for, and then publishes one event: order placed. The shopper is answered. The event is copied into a queue for each listener: fulfilment packs the order when it can, loyalty adds the points later, and large orders go to a fraud check. If the warehouse is down, its orders wait in its queue, and are packed when it comes back. The table says what each one fails like, row by row. The last row is the price. Asynchronous is eventual: the order is packed a little later, and, as we will see, perhaps delivered twice, so the code must be ready for that. Over this course we build the lower half, one piece at a time: a queue, what to do with a message that keeps failing, a function that consumes it, a topic that fans it out, a bus that routes events, a workflow for the payment, and doing each job exactly once. First, the queue.

The first piece is a queue, in S Q S, called book shop fulfilment. The editor shows checkout dot p y. Place records the order in the orders database, in one transaction, as in Course 7. Then, highlighted, it finds the queue and sends one message, order placed, with the order's number, the customer, the books and the total. And that is all: packing and posting are no longer the checkout's business. The role may only send to this queue, never read from it or delete. In the terminal, Terraform makes the queue, and customer c eighteen checks out: order three, nineteen pounds forty nine, and the message is sent. Now a worker, which we play by hand with consume dot p y. A worker receives a message, does the work, and then deletes it, and the delete is how it says it is done. Here the worker crashes before the delete. The side pane follows that message by the clock. At zero seconds, it was received, with a receive count of one. Receiving does not remove it; it hides it, for the queue's visibility timeout of thirty seconds, so no other worker takes the same order while this one works. A receive in that window finds nothing. When the thirty seconds are up, the message is visible again: the next receive gets it with a receive count of two, packs it, and deletes it. One note on the clock: this machine's clock is frozen, so that every run prints the same times. Sleep moves it on, and the timeout then ends in the emulator because its time has passed. The table keeps the queue's promises: at least once, hidden while worked on, done only when deleted. Next, a message that never succeeds.

A message that fails comes back, and is tried again. That is right for a crash, but some messages can never succeed, and without a limit they would come back forever, taking a worker's time on every try. So the editor adds two things to queues dot t f. A second queue, the dead-letter queue, which keeps a message for fourteen days, the longest S Q S allows. And, highlighted, a redrive policy on the fulfilment queue: after a message has been received three times without being deleted, it moves to the dead-letter queue. In the terminal, after the apply, we send a broken order by hand: order nine nine nine, with no books in it. The worker receives it, cannot pack it, and leaves it. Thirty one seconds later it is back, receive count two, and fails again; then receive count three, and fails again. On the fourth receive, the worker finds nothing at all: the queue moved the message to the dead-letter queue instead of handing it out, and reading the dead-letter queue shows order nine nine nine, exactly as it was sent.
