The side pane follows its three tries and the move. The table is the policy, and what happens next. A person reads the dead-letter queue, because a message there means something the code did not expect. Once the cause is fixed, S Q S can move the messages back to the queue they came from, to be worked again. And the count of messages in a dead-letter queue is one of the first alarms worth having, in Course 11. Next, a worker that A W S runs for us.

Running our own worker means running a loop, somewhere, all the time. Lambda can do it instead. The editor shows the function, handler dot p y in functions slash fulfil. Lambda calls it with a batch of messages. For each one, it packs the order; a message it cannot pack is added to batch item failures, highlighted, and the function returns that list. Lambda then deletes every message in the batch except the ones reported, which go back to the queue to be retried, and in the end, to the dead-letter queue. In function dot t f, Terraform builds the function, Python three point one three on arm sixty four, with its own role, allowed to read and delete from this queue and write its logs, and an event source mapping. The mapping is Lambda's own poller: it reads the queue for us and calls the function with up to ten messages, or whatever arrived in five seconds. In the terminal, the mapping is listed, enabled, batch size ten. Two orders are placed, orders four and five, and a third, broken message is sent by hand. The side pane shows what the poller does with them. Now, the honest part, in red. The emulator records the function and the mapping, but it runs neither. So poll dot p y plays the poller: it receives the batch from the queue, builds the event exactly as Lambda builds it, calls the real handler, and deletes what it was not told to keep. The function packs orders four and five; two messages are deleted, and one is left in the queue to retry. The table compares the two consumers. Next, more than one listener for every order.

Back on the shop's map. The checkout column now has its queue and its function, and this section adds the topic, ringed. Fulfilment is not the only part of the shop that cares about an order. Loyalty adds points for every one, and the fraud team wants to look at large ones. Checkout could send three messages, but then every new listener would mean changing checkout. Instead, checkout publishes once, to an S N S topic called book shop orders, and every queue subscribed to the topic gets its own copy. In the terminal, Terraform creates the topic, two new queues, a policy on each queue that lets the topic, and only the topic, write to it, and three subscriptions. One of them has a filter policy: the fraud check receives an order only when its total is five hundred or more. Checkout now publishes instead of sending, and the role's permission changes to match. Then two customers check out. Order six, twenty one pounds ninety eight. And order seven, fifty copies of one book, five hundred and forty nine pounds fifty. Listing what each queue holds, without taking anything, shows the fan out. Fulfilment has both orders. Loyalty has both orders. And the fraud check has only order seven, because order six did not pass its filter. The side pane draws it: one publish, three copies, one filtered. Each listener now works through its own queue, at its own pace, and a slow fraud check never holds up a parcel. Next, events that come from more than one place.

A topic is good when one producer has several listeners. But a shop has many producers. Checkout says an order was placed; the returns desk says a refund was asked for. And listeners care about particular events: the V A T ledger wants orders from the United Kingdom, and nothing else. That is an event bus, in EventBridge. The editor shows events dot t f. A bus called book shop, and two rules, each a pattern. The highlighted rule, U K V A T, matches events from checkout, of type order placed, whose detail says country G B: a pattern can look at any field inside the event. The second rule, refunds, matches refund requested events from the returns desk. Each rule has a target, a queue, and a policy that lets that rule, and only it, write there. In the terminal, three sample events are put on the bus: an order from Great Britain, an order from France, and a refund. The bus accepts all three, with no failures. Looking in the targets: the V A T queue holds the British order, and the refunds queue holds the refund. The French order matched no rule, so it went nowhere, which is exactly what the V A T ledger wants. Then we ask the U K V A T rule directly, with test event pattern, whether it matches the French order, and it answers false. The side pane draws the three events, the bus, the rules and their targets. The table sets the topic and the bus side by side. Next, a job with several steps that must happen in order.

Taking a payment is several steps in order. Reserve the copies. Charge the card. If that worked, ship. If it did not, give the copies back. Coding that order, with its retries and its undo, inside one function would hide it; Step Functions makes it a state machine instead, a definition we can read. The editor shows the payment step in checkout dot a s l dot j s o n. It is a task, a Lambda function. Highlighted, its retry: when the provider times out, try again after two seconds, then after four, at most twice. And its catch: any other failure, or a timeout after the retries, goes to release stock, and then to order failed. Each step is its own small function, in steps dot p y, and Terraform makes the four functions and the state machine, which the emulator reports as active. Now the honest part. The emulator records the state machine but runs none of its steps, so a small tool walks the definition: each task calls the step's real code, and the stock changes are real, in the emulator's table. Only the payment provider's answers are stand-ins, written in the tool. For order ten, the provider times out twice. The terminal shows the retries, at two seconds and at four, the charge succeeding at six seconds, the order shipped, and the execution succeeded. For order eleven, the card is declined. Retrying cannot help, so the catch sends it to release stock, which gives the two copies back, and the execution fails, on purpose, with order failed. The side pane draws the machine, and the table is order eleven's path. Next, the problem every asynchronous system meets: doing a job exactly once.

A standard S Q S queue delivers every message at least once, and once in a while, twice. A producer that times out and sends again does the same. For fulfilment, twice means two parcels. The fix is to make the work idempotent: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The editor shows how, in the fulfil function. Before it packs an order, it claims it, highlighted: it writes a key, fulfil hash the order's number, into a DynamoDB table, on the condition that the key does not exist yet. The first delivery writes the key and packs. A second delivery finds the key taken, the write is refused, and the function skips the order, and reports success, so the duplicate is deleted rather than retried. Terraform adds the table, with a seven day time to live on its keys, longer than any message can be redelivered, and allows the function's role to write to it. In the terminal, the function is rebuilt and applied. Then we send order twelve twice, exactly the same message, as a duplicate delivery would. The poller picks up the batch, with the two orders still waiting from the fan out, and the two copies of order twelve. Orders six, seven and twelve are packed, and the second copy of order twelve is skipped as a duplicate. Scanning the table shows one key per order packed. The side pane draws the two deliveries meeting at the key. The condition is checked and written in one step, so even two copies arriving at the same moment cannot both win. Next, choosing between all of these.

This course built four ways for the parts of the shop to talk without waiting, and the frame places each one on the finished checkout. Checkout records the order directly, because it needs that answer now: a direct call is still right when the caller needs the result. The payment is a workflow, in Step Functions, because its steps must happen in order, with retries, and with an undo when the card is declined; in this course we started it by hand. The order placed event goes to a topic, in S N S, because several listeners must all hear it, and adding one is a subscription, not a change to checkout. Each listener reads its own queue, in S Q S: fulfilment, through its function, which claims every order once; loyalty; and the fraud check, which sees only large orders. Below, the bus, in EventBridge: events from checkout and the returns desk, routed by what they say, to the V A T and refunds queues. The table is the rule of thumb. A queue, when one consumer works through jobs at its own pace and must retry. A topic, when one event has several listeners. A bus, when there are many sources and the routing depends on the content. A workflow, when steps must run in order with retries and an undo. And a plain call, when the answer is needed now. That completes Course 8: the checkout no longer waits for anything but its own order. Next course, the shop ships through a pipeline, into two accounts.

Production is coming, and it needs the same network as development. Copying four files and editing them would leave two versions to keep in step forever. A module is the answer: a folder of Terraform that takes inputs, so one piece of code can be used many times. The network from Course 5, the V P C, nine subnets, two route tables, the gateways and the S three endpoint, moves into modules slash network, with two inputs: a name, and the V P C's range, from which each subnet's range is now worked out. The editor shows what the root keeps, network dot t f. A module block, highlighted, calls the module with development's values. But this changes every resource's address. The V P C was aws V P C dot shop; now it is module dot network, aws V P C dot this. To Terraform, a new address means a new resource: without help, the plan would destroy the network and build another, with the tasks and the database inside it. So each resource gets a moved block, highlighted: from the old address, to the new one. It says the thing is the same; only its name in the code changed. In the terminal, init installs the module. The plan lists every resource as moved, the V P C among them, and ends with zero to add, zero to change, zero to destroy. The side pane draws the root calling the module, and the table shows three addresses before and after. Nothing in the account changed. Next, the same module, in a second account.

Production gets its own account, one one one one, two two two two, three three three three, so that a mistake in development can never reach it. The editor shows its root, envs slash prod slash main dot t f. Two parts are highlighted. Its state lives in a bucket in production's own account, not in development's. And it calls the very same network module, with one input changed: production's range is ten dot forty, not ten dot twenty, so the two could be connected one day. Its provider reaches production through a role: for now, the administrator role that A W S Organizations creates in every account it makes, reached from the developer's own sign in. In section four, the pipeline gets a narrower role of its own. In the terminal, a tiny root makes production's state bucket first, with local state, the way Course 3 made development's. Then production's root is initialised and applied: twenty seven resources, the whole network. Last, the same question asked of each account: which V P Cs are called book shop? Development answers with its account and ten dot twenty. Production, asked through its profile, answers with its own account and ten dot forty. The side pane draws one module feeding two roots, each with its own account and its own state. The table says what differs and what does not: the code is identical, the inputs differ, and a mistake stays where it was made. Next, the path every change will take to get there.

Until now, every change to the shop was applied from a laptop. That works for one person; it does not work for a team, and it should never be how production changes. A delivery pipeline gives every change the same path, and the frame draws it in two rows. Above, a pull request, where nothing changes yet. A commit on a branch is checked: is the Terraform formatted, and is it valid? Then it is planned against development, and the plan is posted on the pull request, so a reviewer reads exactly what will change, before anything does. Below, what happens on merge. The reviewed change is applied to development, in a real account. Only if that works does the pipeline go on, and then it waits: a second person must approve the production environment. Then it applies to production. The table goes stage by stage: what each one proves, and what blocks it. Formatting and validation catch mistakes in seconds. The plan shows the change. The review puts a person in front of it. Applying to development proves it works before production sees it, and the approval means someone chose to ship now. The note at the bottom is the security point: no job holds a stored key. Each asks GitHub for a token that lasts minutes, and trades it for a role in its account. The next two sections build those roles, and the workflow file itself.

A pipeline that changes two accounts needs credentials for both, and the worst place to keep them is in the pipeline, as long lived keys, where one leak gives everything away. Instead, each job proves who it is, and gets credentials for an hour. The side pane follows one job. It asks GitHub for a token: a signed statement that says which repository it comes from and which branch or environment it runs in. It hands the token to S T S, with assume role with web identity. S T S checks GitHub's signature, and that the token is meant for it, and that its subject matches the role's trust policy, and only then returns credentials for the role. The editor shows that trust policy, in the new pipeline module. It trusts GitHub's O I D C provider, which the module registers in the account, and, highlighted, only the subjects passed in. Development's role trusts runs on main, and pull requests, which only plan. Production's trusts a single subject: a run in GitHub's production environment, the one a reviewer must approve. Its permissions are the shop's own services, and I A M changes only to roles whose names start with book shop: never a person, and never another team's role. In the terminal, the module is applied in development, then in production, and production's trust policy is read back: the web identity action, the audience, the subject that ends in environment production, and the provider. The table sums up who may assume which. The red note is the honest part: the emulator stores the provider and the trust, but does not check tokens; the exchange is GitHub's and A W S's documentation. Next, the workflow that uses these roles.

Now the pipeline itself, as a file in the repository: dot github slash workflows slash infra dot y m l. The editor shows its jobs. Check runs on every pull request and every push: terraform format, check, highlighted, which fails if any file is not formatted the standard way, and validate, which fails if the configuration does not make sense. Plan dev runs on a pull request, after check, assumes development's pipeline role, and plans. Apply dev runs on main and applies to development. And apply prod waits for apply dev, and then for the production environment, highlighted: GitHub holds the job until a reviewer approves it, and that environment's name is exactly what production's role trusts. In the terminal, a small tool reads the jobs out of the file, and then we run the same checks locally, before ever pushing. The code is formatted. It is valid. A plan with detailed exit code returns zero, which means nothing would change: what is in the code is what is in development. To see the gate close, we write a badly aligned scratch file. Format check now lists it, and exits with three: in the pipeline, that is a red check, and the pull request cannot merge until it is fixed. The side pane is the gate as the file declares it, and the table is what each check answered. One honest note: this workflow has not run on GitHub; it is the shop's file, run here by hand. Next, what to do when the account and the code disagree.

Between two sections, sam did two things in the console. During a slow evening, the fulfilment queue's visibility timeout went up to sixty seconds. And the returns desk needed a queue, so sam made one by hand: book shop returns. Neither is in the code. This is drift: the account no longer matches what the code says it should be, and the side pane names the three versions of the shop. The account is what is really there. The state is Terraform's record of it, and every plan first refreshes the state from the account. Then it compares the result with the code, and proposes whatever makes the account match the code. In the terminal, the plan finds the timeout at sixty, and puts it back to thirty: the code wins, so a console change that matters belongs in the code. The returns queue is different: it should stay, so the editor adopts it. An import block, highlighted, names the real queue, and the resource block below says what it should be. The plan reads the queue and shows what would change. One line deserves a look: the maximum message size. A queue made by hand got A W S's default of one mebibyte, and Terraform's resource defaults to two hundred and fifty six kibibytes, so the plan would shrink it. Read it before you apply; if the returns desk needs bigger messages, say so in the code. The plan imports one and changes three. The third is the fulfil function's policy: it reads the queue being changed, so Terraform cannot know it until the apply, and the apply leaves it as it was. The timeout reads back as thirty. The table sums up what was found and what happened to it. Next, the changes a plan cannot make in place.

Some changes cannot be made in place. The loyalty team renamed its service points, and a queue's name is fixed when the queue is made: to rename it, Terraform must make a new queue and remove the old one. The question is in which order, and the side pane draws both. Terraform's default is on the left: remove the old queue, then make the new one. In between, there is nothing to deliver to, and an order placed in that moment is lost to the loyalty team. On the right is the order we want: make the new queue first, subscribe it, and only then remove the old one. For a moment both queues get a copy of each order, and Course 8's idempotency is why that is safe. The editor shows how to ask for it. The name changes to book shop points, and a lifecycle block, highlighted, sets create before destroy. The queue's subscription and its policy point at the queue, so they are replaced too, and they need the same lifecycle; without it, the old subscription went first in our first try. The new subscription also waits for the new queue's policy, so the topic can deliver from its very first message. In the terminal, the plan shows the new name forcing a replacement, and the apply adds three and destroys three. The table lists the order it really ran in, read from the output: everything new first, everything old after. Some things should never be replaced at all. The orders database holds every order, so database dot t f gives it prevent destroy. When we ask for a replacement anyway, with plan dash replace, Terraform stops with an error before anything changes. Protecting a resource is a line of code, and so is the decision to remove that protection. Next, the same care for the app itself: releasing a new version.

Infrastructure goes through the pipeline; so does the app. And sooner or later a release is bad. Here, version one point two point zero fails two requests in every hundred. The error alarm notices after two minutes, and the release is rolled back. The question is how many shoppers see an error before then, and that depends on how the new version was put in front of them. The left of the frame names four ways. All at once: every task is replaced together. Rolling: one task of seven is replaced each minute. Blue green: a whole new set of tasks is started, and traffic switches to it; going back is one switch, but everyone was on the new version. And canary: one tenth of the traffic goes to the new version first, and the rest only after it has proved itself. The plot comes from a small model, labelled as one, at the evening peak of four hundred and twenty requests a second. All at once climbs fastest: about a thousand failed requests before the alarm. Rolling grows as more tasks are replaced: about two hundred. The canary stays flat and low: about a hundred, because only a tenth of shoppers ever met the bad version. The terminal shows the model's own output. The table is the trade. All at once costs nothing and exposes everyone. Rolling needs room for one more task. Blue green needs twice the tasks for a while, and makes going back instant. A canary needs traffic splitting and an alarm you trust. That completes Course 9: the shop ships through a pipeline, and a bad release reaches few people. Next course, it reports on what it sold.

The finance team has a question: what did we sell yesterday? The orders database could answer it, but it is the wrong place to ask. The frame starts with what the database is for. It holds the shop's state: one row per order, changed by every checkout, built for many small reads and writes, each touching a few rows. A sales report is the opposite shape of work: it reads a whole day, or a whole month, once, and adds it up. Run against the database, it competes with every checkout for the same machine, at exactly the moment the shop is busy. So history leaves the database. Along the top, the path this course builds. Every night, an export job copies yesterday's orders out of the database into a lake: a bucket of files, one folder per day, written once and never changed. A catalog describes those files: their columns, and how they are split into days. And a query engine reads only the days a question asks about. The first table sorts questions by where they belong. Is order twelve paid? How many copies are left? Those are about now, and the database answers them. What sold yesterday, and how September compared with August, are about the past, and the lake answers them. The second table puts the two shapes side by side: many small changes against few large reads, rows against columns, an instance running all day against storage and a charge per query. Next, the export itself.

Terraform has made the lake: a private bucket, book shop lake, in the development account. Before anything can be exported by day, every order needs a day, so the first command in the terminal applies a migration that gives each order the time it was placed. The shop's real orders are the handful from Courses 7 and 8, far too few for a report, so the next command writes a month of trade that we made up for the course, and says so: thirty thousand orders in September, seeded, so every run writes the same month. Then the export job, open in the editor. It asks the database for one day's order lines at a time, highlighted: placed on or after that day, and before the next. It turns them into a table with a fixed schema, so the price column means the same thing in every file, and writes it as Parquet, highlighted: a file that stores each column together, compressed. Then it puts the file in the lake, under a key that names the day, highlighted: order history, slash, d t equals the date. Thirty files, just over sixty thousand order lines, under six hundred kibibytes for the month. Listing the lake counts thirty folders, one per day, and the first holds a single file. The side pane follows one night: the database, the job, and the bucket's layout, with September the thirtieth newest. Those d t equals folders are the point. A question about one day can now open one folder and ignore the rest, as long as something tells the query engine how the files are laid out. Next, that catalog.

Files in a bucket are just files. A query engine needs to know what is in them: which columns, of which types, and how they are split. That description lives in the Glue Data Catalog, and the editor declares it: a database called book shop lake, and a table, order history, over the lake's files. The files do not move; the table only describes them. Its partition key is d t, highlighted near the bottom: the day in each folder's name. Above it, the table's parameters, highlighted, switch on partition projection. Without it, every new day would have to be added to the catalog, by a crawler or by hand, before a query could see it. With it, the engine works the folder out for itself: it takes the day from the query's filter and puts it into the location template, highlighted, order history slash d t equals the day. Tomorrow's export needs no change here: its folder is simply there. In the terminal, Terraform adds the database and the table, and the table's columns are read back from the catalog: order I D, customer, book, quantity, price, and when it was placed. The side pane shows how a query will use this. A filter names a day, the table turns it into a folder, and only that folder is read. The table below compares each column with the type the export job wrote into the files: they match, because both were fixed on purpose. One honest note: the emulator stores the table and its parameters; projection itself is applied by the query engine. Next, asking the question.

Athena runs S Q L over the lake's files where they lie. There is nothing to keep running between questions, and each query is charged by the data it scans. Terraform has made a workgroup for reports: it says where results go, and sets a limit, one gibibyte, that no query may scan past, a guard against an expensive mistake. The editor holds the question as a file: the five books that took the most money yesterday, September the thirtieth, highlighted in the filter on d t. In the terminal, the file is handed to Athena, which accepts it and returns a query I D. Here is the honest part. The emulator records the query; it does not run it. So the next two commands run the same file a second way. The lake's files are copied down, and a small tool hands the same S Q L to Duck D B, an engine that reads Parquet on a laptop, with the table defined exactly as the catalog defines it. The answer comes back: book two thousand and eighteen first, with a hundred and ninety nine copies and just over five thousand one hundred pounds, then four more. The last line is Duck D B's own account of the run: it read one file of thirty. The side pane draws that. Thirty day folders, twenty nine of them greyed: the filter on d t ruled them out before a single byte was read. On Athena, that is the bill: one day scanned instead of a month. Partitioning by the column you filter on most is the cheapest optimisation a lake has. Next, data that does not wait for the night: a stream.

Orders can wait for the night. Clicks are different: the marketing team wants to see which books people are looking at now, so every page view goes into a stream as it happens. The editor declares it, a Kinesis data stream called book shop clicks, with two shards, highlighted. A shard is a lane: each takes up to a thousand records a second, so more traffic means more shards. The stream keeps every record for twenty four hours, also highlighted, so a consumer that falls behind can catch up. Each record carries a partition key, and here the key is the shopper's session. The key decides the shard, which means one session's clicks always land in the same shard, in the order they happened. In the terminal, a small tool sends a thousand made up clicks from fifty sessions, and reports where each went. Five hundred and ninety six landed in shard zero, and four hundred and four in shard one. Not an even split, because the split follows the keys, and some sessions click more than others: a busy key makes a busy shard. No session was split across the two. Then each shard is read back from its start. The plot below is a model, labelled as one. One consumer per shard reads six hundred clicks a second, and the evening peaks at sixteen hundred. With two shards, each gets eight hundred: the consumer falls behind from about ten past six, and by ten to seven it is nearly seven minutes behind. With four shards, it never falls behind at all. Lag is the number to watch on a stream. Next, choosing where the shop's history should be answered.

The shop now answers its sales questions from a lake, with Athena. That is one of three common ways, and the frame places them side by side over the same files. Along the top, the lake and the catalog: the same Parquet files, and one table definition, which any of the three can read. On the left, querying in place: Athena, what this course built. Nothing runs between queries, and each one costs the data it scans. In the middle, a warehouse: Redshift, where the data is loaded into tables kept ready for many repeated queries from many people, the dashboards a business opens every morning. On the right, a cluster: E M R, which runs your own code, usually Spark, for the transformations that S Q L cannot express. The table makes the choice concrete. Athena fits a few questions a day, asked in S Q L, and costs nothing when nobody asks. Redshift fits when reports become dashboards that dozens of people refresh, because then keeping data warm beats scanning files every time. E M R fits jobs rather than queries: cleaning, joining and reshaping large data with code. The last row is the shop today: thirty thousand orders a month and a few reports a day is Athena's shape, and the other two wait until the questions change. That completes Course 10: the shop knows what it sold, without slowing a single checkout. Next course, operating it: knowing when something is wrong, and what to do about it.

Last night, between twenty past six and twenty five to seven, some shoppers could not pay. Nobody noticed until the morning. This course is about noticing, and about what to do next, and it starts with the three kinds of evidence a running system leaves. On the left, a metric: the share of requests that failed, five minutes at a time. It says something was wrong, and when, and how much: around one request in eight, for fifteen minutes. It does not say which requests. Top right, a log line, exactly as the app writes one: a post to checkout, answered with five oh three. Logs say which requests failed, one by one, but there are thousands of them. Below it, a trace of one checkout, and this one is an example, because the shop does not collect traces yet. It breaks one request into the steps it took: the load balancer, two milliseconds; the database, four; and the payments A P I, three seconds, until it timed out. That is where the time went. The table joins them. The metric answers whether something is wrong and since when; the log answers which requests; the trace answers where. Together, they point at the payments A P I. The rest of this course builds the shop's version of each: metrics made from its logs, an alarm that wakes someone for the right reasons, a record of who changed what, keys, a firewall, backups, and one incident handled from start to finish.

The app already writes one line of J S O N for every request, and E C S already sends every line to the log group book shop slash app, kept for thirty days. Turning those lines into numbers needs no change to the app: a metric filter. The editor declares two. Requests counts every line with a status. Errors five x x counts the lines whose status is five hundred or more, highlighted: failures that are the shop's fault, not the shopper's. Each filter watches the app's log group, and publishes a metric in the book shop namespace, also highlighted, a count each minute. In the terminal, a tool writes last night into the real log group: an hour of requests, made up for the course and seeded, two hundred a minute, with the payments A P I down for fifteen minutes. Then an honest step. The emulator stores metric filters but never runs them, so a second tool reads the events back, applies the same two rules, and publishes the counts, as CloudWatch would. Twelve thousand requests, three hundred and ninety six errors, the worst minute at eighteen twenty two, with thirty three failures in two hundred. Last, the metric is read back from CloudWatch, ten minutes at a time. The side pane follows one line, from the app to the log group, through a filter, to a number, and the plot shows those ten minute sums: nothing, then two hundred and sixty four, then a hundred and thirty two, then nothing. A metric is something an alarm can watch. Next, deciding when it should.

An alarm on the raw error count would wake someone for every bad minute, and teach them to ignore it. A better question starts from an objective. The shop's is that ninety nine and a half percent of requests succeed, measured over thirty days. What is left, half a percent, is the error budget: the failures the shop can afford. The useful question is how fast that budget is burning. A burn rate of one spends it in exactly thirty days. The editor sets two alarms on the same ratio, errors divided by requests, highlighted. The fast one fires when five minutes burn at fourteen point four times the rate, which is an error rate above seven point two percent: at that pace, two percent of the month's budget goes in an hour, and someone should look now. The slow one watches the whole hour, at six times: a quieter problem that would empty the budget in five days. Both notify the topic book shop alerts, highlighted, which emails alex. In the terminal, the two alarms are read back with their thresholds. The emulator stores alarms but does not evaluate them, so a tool applies the same thresholds to last night's metrics. From eighteen twenty to eighteen thirty five, the burn rate was between twenty four and twenty nine: the fast alarm would have fired three times. Over the hour, three point three percent of requests failed, six point six times the budget's pace: the slow alarm too. The plot shows each five minutes against the fast threshold. Next, finding out who changed what.

In Course 9, sam changed a queue in the console, and the plan found the drift. It did not say who did it, or when. CloudTrail does: it records every call made to A W S in the account, by a person, a pipeline or a service, and delivers the records to a bucket. The editor shows the trail. It covers every Region, highlighted, because an attacker would choose the one nobody watches, and it includes global services such as I A M. Log file validation, also highlighted, adds a signed digest every hour, so a record that was edited or deleted afterwards can be proved to have been. Above it, a bucket of its own, whose policy lets CloudTrail, and only CloudTrail, write into it. In the terminal, the trail is read back: multi Region, validation on, and logging. The side pane follows one call, from sam's console to the trail to the bucket, and the table below is one record. Here is the honest part: the emulator records no events, so this record is the shape A W S documents, filled in with sam's change from Course 9. The event time; the service, S Q S; the action, set queue attributes; who, a developer session named sam; from which address; and what was asked: a visibility timeout of sixty seconds on the fulfilment queue. Every one of those fields is searchable, so who changed this is a question with an answer. Next, protecting the data itself.

The lake holds every order the shop has taken. If its files were copied, encryption at rest is what keeps them unreadable, and the question is who holds the key. Here, the shop does: a key in K M S, the Key Management Service, created by the editor. Its key policy, above this view, lets the account administer it and lets the app's role use it, and nobody else. Rotation is on, highlighted: new key material every year, with old data still readable. Below, the lake bucket's default encryption names that key, highlighted, so every new object is encrypted with it. How that works is called envelope encryption, and the side pane draws it. The key itself never leaves K M S. To write, a service asks K M S for a data key, and gets it twice: in plain, and encrypted under the key. It encrypts the data with the plain copy, drops it, and stores the encrypted copy beside the data. To read, it sends that encrypted data key back to K M S, which first checks the key policy, and only then returns the plain key. In the terminal, a small tool does exactly that by hand. A two hundred and fifty six bit data key. An order encrypted into sixty seven bytes, stored with ninety six bytes of encrypted data key; the plain key, dropped. Then K M S decrypts the data key, and the order reads back. Revoke the role's access in the key policy, and every object it protects becomes unreadable to it at once. Next, the front door.

Every request to the shop arrives at the load balancer from the internet, and some are not shoppers. A W S W A F, a web application firewall, reads each request before the shop does, and the editor gives it two rules. The first, highlighted, is a rule group A W S maintains: the common rule set, which recognises well known attacks, such as S Q L injection in a query string, requests with no user agent, and oversized bodies. A W S updates it as new attacks appear; the shop only chooses to use it. The second is the shop's own: no single address may send more than a thousand requests in five minutes, highlighted. Beyond that, its requests are blocked until it slows down. An association, below the view, attaches the rules to the load balancer. In the terminal, the rules are read back from the load balancer itself, in order: the common rules first, then the rate rule. The emulator stores the rules and their association; it inspects no requests. The side pane is the point of this section: W A F is one layer of four, and each stops something different. W A F stops attack patterns and floods. The load balancer accepts only H T T P S, with modern T L S. The app's security group accepts only the load balancer. And the app checks every input itself, because only it knows what a valid order looks like. No layer is enough alone. Next, being able to get the data back.

Multi A Z protects the orders database from a failed machine. It does not protect it from a bad migration, a deleted table, or an attacker with the right credentials, because those changes are copied to the standby at once. That needs backups, and A W S Backup takes them on a plan, as the editor declares. Every night at three, the quietest hour, highlighted, it backs up what the selection names: the orders database, and the carts and stock tables. Each backup goes into a vault encrypted with the shop's own key, and is kept for thirty five days, highlighted. Then a copy action, also highlighted, sends a copy to a vault in the audit account, seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine, kept for ninety days. Someone who takes over the development account can delete its backups; they cannot reach the audit account's. In the terminal, the plan's rule is read back, nightly at three, and so is the selection: the database and both tables. The emulator stores the plan and takes no backups, and the frame says so. Now the most important line on screen, at the bottom of the side pane: a backup is only proved by a restore. Every quarter, the drill restores last night's recovery point as a new instance, runs the app's checks against it, and writes down how long it took. That time, measured, is the shop's real recovery time. Next, an incident, from start to finish.

Fourteen minutes past nine, on a Monday evening. Credentials for a session of the app's role turn up in a public chat. The terminal plays both sides. First, the leaked session is created and used: it lists the catalog. Deleting the role would stop it, and stop the shop too, because every running task uses the same role. Rotating nothing helps either: a role session is valid until it expires, up to an hour. A W S's answer is the policy in the editor. A deny, highlighted, on everything, for any session of this role whose token was issued before twenty one fifteen, also highlighted. Sessions issued after it are not affected, and each running task simply fetches a fresh one. Two minutes later, Terraform applies it. Then the leaked credentials try again, and are refused: access denied. And a fresh session, the kind a task would get, lists the catalog as before. This is real I A M evaluation in the emulator, the token's issue time against the policy's date. The side pane names the four phases every incident goes through. Detect: someone noticed. Contain: stop the damage without stopping the shop, which is what this policy did. Eradicate: find how the credentials leaked, and the trail from section four is where to look. Recover: confirm the shop works, then write down what happened and what will change, without blame. The table is the evening as the terminal showed it. Next, the biggest failure of all.

Everything so far survives a failed machine, or even a failed availability zone. The last question is the rarest and the largest: what if a whole Region is unavailable for a day? A W S's disaster recovery guidance names four strategies, and the frame orders them from left to right, by how fast they recover, which is also what each keeps running in a second Region. Backup and restore keeps only backups there, and rebuilds everything when needed: recovery in hours. Pilot light copies the data continuously, but keeps the servers off until they are needed: tens of minutes. Warm standby runs a small but complete copy of the shop all the time, ready to grow: minutes. And active active runs two full shops, both serving shoppers, so losing one loses almost nothing. The table puts numbers on the trade: how long recovery takes, how much data can be lost, and what keeps running, and costing, in the second Region. Those times are the guidance's orders of magnitude, not measurements. The last row is honest about the shop today. It is at backup and restore, with copies in another account, but not yet in another Region. For a small shop, hours of downtime once in many years may be an acceptable price. The point is that it is a decision, made in advance, with its cost and its recovery time written down. That completes Course 11: the shop is observed, audited, encrypted, backed up and recoverable. Next course: measuring, tuning, and deciding what comes next.

The shop lives in London, and so far every request has travelled there. For a shopper in Sydney, that is about two hundred and eighty milliseconds for the round trip alone, before the app does anything. A C D N, a content delivery network, keeps copies of pages at edge locations near the shoppers. On the map, CloudFront joins the edge, in front of everything. In the terminal, Terraform adds three things: a distribution whose origin is the load balancer, reached only over H T T P S, and two cache policies. Book pages, the default, are cached for up to five minutes, so a price change shows within five minutes. Anything under slash checkout is never cached and accepts every method, because an order must always reach London. The distribution reads back as deployed, with its own cloudfront dot net name, and the one special path is listed: slash checkout. The plot is a model, labelled as one, of a book page seen from Sydney. Without a C D N, three hundred and ten milliseconds. With one, it depends on how often the edge already has the page. With no hits it is slightly slower than going direct, because of the extra hop; at ninety percent hits, under fifty milliseconds. So the setting that matters is how long a page may be cached, and that is a business decision: how stale may a price be? Five minutes, here. The emulator stores the distribution and serves nothing, and the terminal is labelled so. Next, measuring before changing anything else.

Course 6 told the shop to add tasks when they are sixty percent busy. Why not ninety, and save money? The answer is a curve, and this frame draws it from a simulation, labelled as one, of a single task. Each request takes ten milliseconds of work on average, which is Course 6's hundred requests a second, and requests arrive at random, as shoppers do. The terminal shows the simulation's output, from ten percent busy to ninety five. The plot shows two lines. The median, the typical request, rises gently. The ninety ninth percentile, the slowest request in a hundred, is the one that matters, because at the shop's traffic that is thousands of shoppers an hour. It is about a hundred milliseconds at sixty percent busy. At eighty percent, it has doubled, to over two hundred. At ninety five, it is near seven hundred: the shopper notices. Latency does not grow in proportion to load. It bends, sharply, somewhere past seventy percent, because requests start to queue behind each other, and the queue grows faster than the load. That bend is the knee, and the dashed line at sixty percent is where the shop scales out, before it. The table turns it into a habit: before tuning anything, measure the ninety ninth percentile at peak; change one thing; measure again. A change that makes the average better and the tail worse has made the shop slower for the shoppers who notice. Next, what all of this costs.

What does the finished shop cost to run? The lab on screen answers with the shop's own quantities, for a month in production: four tasks on average, a Multi A Z database, one N A T gateway, two shards, and the rest. The rates, though, are hypothetical: round numbers of about the right size, chosen for the course and labelled so. A W S's real prices change and differ by Region, so check the pricing pages before deciding anything. The total comes to about two hundred and thirty four dollars a month. The bar chart shows the six largest lines. Compute, the Fargate tasks, comes first, as it usually does. The surprise is second: the N A T gateway, almost a fifth of the bill, because it charges by the hour and again for every gigabyte it carries. Then the database and the load balancer, which run all day whether anyone shops or not. The table below names the levers. Committing to a year of compute and database use, through a Savings Plan or reserved instances, saves about twenty two dollars a month here. Sending S three and image traffic through V P C endpoints instead of the N A T gateway cuts that line. Right sizing comes after measuring, as the last section said, never before. And development does not need to run at night or at weekends, which is two thirds of its hours. Next, telling development's costs from production's.

Since Course 3, every resource has carried the same default tags, including app and env. Tags are not part of the bill until they are activated as cost allocation tags, and the editor does that for both, highlighted. In the terminal, they read back as active. From then on, the bill can be split by them, and a small tool reads a month of it. October's figures are made up for the course, in the shape a Cost Explorer export has: a cost per day, per service, per environment. Production, two hundred and thirteen dollars, two thirds of the total. Development, ninety nine. And two findings the tags made visible. First, development passed its twenty dollar budget, the one from Course 3, on the seventh of October. That is what a budget is for: not a cap, an alarm, and it emailed alex. Second, a rule that flags any day costing more than twice its usual: on the twenty first and twenty second, development's N A T gateway cost four and a half, then nearly four times its normal day. Something in development pulled a lot of data through the N A T gateway, perhaps images or packages downloaded over and over. Without tags, it would have been a small bump in one total; with them, it has a service, an environment and a date, which is enough to ask the right person. The emulator keeps no bill, and the note says so. Next, writing down a decision so nobody has to guess it later.

Someone will ask, sooner or later, why the orders are in RDS PostgreSQL rather than Aurora or DynamoDB. An architecture decision record answers once, in a short file kept beside the code: docs slash A D R, zero zero one. The editor shows its heart: two tables. Musts first. An option that fails one is out, however good it is otherwise. All three can commit an order and its lines together, keep stock from going below zero, and restore to any second of the last thirty five days. But DynamoDB alone fails the last must, highlighted: the reports' S Q L would not run unchanged. Then wants, each with a weight from one to three, and each option scored from one to five. Monthly cost at today's load weighs most, highlighted. The terminal shows a small tool that reads the two tables from the record itself and does the arithmetic: RDS PostgreSQL, thirty five of forty; Aurora Serverless, thirty; DynamoDB, out. The scores are the team's judgement, not facts, and that is the point of writing them down: the next person can disagree with a number instead of a vague memory. The decision, highlighted, is to stay on RDS PostgreSQL, with a condition for revisiting it: ten times today's orders. The side pane is the method, which works for any choice: musts filter, weighted wants rank, and the record is kept. Next, the whole shop, judged.

Here is the finished shop, on the map that has followed it since Course 3: every part the course built in colour, and what it chose not to build, greyed in place. A W S's Well Architected Framework reviews a system against six pillars, and the table judges this one. Operational excellence: everything is declared in Terraform and shipped through a pipeline, with alarms on what matters; next, a short runbook for each alarm. Security: roles with only what they need, keys the shop controls, a firewall and an audit trail; next, threat detection with GuardDuty and Security Hub. Reliability: three availability zones, a queue that absorbs failures, and backups copied to another account; next, a N A T gateway in every zone, and a restore drill on the calendar. Performance: scaling before the knee, a C D N, and a lake that keeps reports off the database; next, measuring the ninety ninth percentile at peak, regularly. Cost: tags, a budget and a bill that is understood; next, a commitment, and development switched off at night. Sustainability: the functions already run on Graviton; the tasks could too. Below the table, an order for the next steps: a restore drill first, because until one is done the backups are a hope; then a N A T gateway in every zone; then a commitment, once a month of real bills says how much. The note matters most: what is greyed on the map is not a list of failures. A cache, more N A T gateways, a second Region: each is a decision for the shop to make with its own numbers. That completes Course 12, and the shop: built, secured, observed, and understood.
